lines: A little terrier just inspected my shoes. I think I passed.
Biscuit, is it? He walked me to the fountain. Very kind.
The terrier sat down and refused to go on. I agreed with him.
A dog wagged at me from across the square. I feel chosen.
That terrier has a very important stick. I gave it a nod.
A gull is following me. I think it likes my hat.
The gulls here sit in a row on the railing. Like a choir.
One gull, one lamp post, one perfect afternoon.
A gull just looked at my map. It seemed to know the way.
There is a cat on that wall. It has not moved since lunch.
I said bonjour to a cat. It said nothing, very politely.
Every wall here has its own cat. It must be a rule.
The cat found the only warm stone. Clever cat.
Someone is playing accordion somewhere. I am following it.
I lost the accordion behind the café. Found a fig tree.
A radio in a window is playing a waltz. I slowed down for it.
I hummed the café tune all the way up the hill yesterday.
Somebody practising piano upstairs. Same bar, getting better.
Three lines of a crossword, one hour of promenade. Fair trade.
Eleven across: a calm place by the sea. Five letters. Here?
I bring my crossword down every afternoon. I never finish it.
Henri gave me a crossword clue. I think it was a riddle.
My pencil lives behind my ear now. Very holiday.
I brought a novel. I have read the same page four times.
Chapter three, a bench, and a breeze. Perfect order.
I keep a notebook of nice things. It is filling up fast.
I pressed a bougainvillea flower in my book. Page eighty.
My little sketchbook is all doors. The doors here are blue.
I tried to sketch the fountain. It came out as a cake.
Today I am counting cypresses. Fourteen, so far.
I collect postcards of places I am standing in. Silly, yes.
I have photographed this window box twice. It deserves it.
My afternoon routine: walk, stop, smile, walk.
Down the hill at half past two. Back up when the shade says.
I take the long way to the kiosk. There is no short way here.
I always turn left at the fountain. Today I turned right.
Oh, this street again. I am delighted to see it.
I have been lost three times today. Each time, nicer.
Pardon, is this the promenade? Oh, it is all promenade.
I followed the smell of oranges and found a staircase.
My map is upside down. The town looks lovely either way.
A little alley, a little cat, a little fig. Wonderful.
The shutters are all half closed. The whole town naps.
It is siesta hour. I am walking very quietly.
The afternoon here smells of warm stone and lemons.
Long shadows already. The cypresses are showing off.
The sea is that colour again. I do not have a word for it.
The palms are swaying very slowly. I am copying them.
Henri is watering the lemon tree. It looks very proud.
Henri tipped his hat at me. I do not have a hat to tip.
Odile told me the whole history of that bench. Lovely bench.
Odile knew my name before I told her. Wonderful town.
Lucie rang her bell at me. I waved. I think that is the custom.
A bicycle went by with a baguette in the basket. Of course.
Léo told me there are ninety steps up to the church. I believe him.
Two children are racing round the fountain. Both winning.
Théo says he is working. He is holding a croissant.
Camille pointed out a gecko. I would have missed it.
The waiter whistled at me. Kindly. It meant sit down.
Marcel says the tarte is a crime to skip. I will obey.
Someone in the café laughed, and then everyone did.
I had a lemon ice at three. A second one seems reasonable.
Afternoon coffee at the kiosk. Tiny cup, enormous joy.
I ate an apricot standing up. It felt very French.
The bakery has one croissant left. I am leaving it for luck.
I bought a peach for later. Later is already now.
I said merci correctly today. Twice. I am very pleased.
My French is three words and a smile. It works beautifully.
In the old town we have one bench. Here, you have dozens.
My aunt said I would like it here. My aunt is always right.
I wrote a postcard to myself. It just says: stay longer.
The fountain has a little rainbow in it at this hour.
Someone painted that door yellow. Bless them.
Washing on a line, blowing like flags. A very good flag.
The church bell rang four. Nobody hurried. I love that.
Four o'clock. The town gets slower, and so do I.
Half past three is the quietest hour. I save it for walking.
My shoes and I agree: one more lap of the square.
I am learning which cobbles wobble. It is like a song.
I found a bench in the shade. Then a better one.
Every window box has geraniums. Someone is very organised.
The zinc roofs shine like spoons this time of day.
A lizard and I shared a sunny step. He left first.
A butterfly has been leading me for a while. Fine by me.
There is a hammock in that garden. I am trying not to stare.
The ice cream stand has a flavour called lavender. Brave.
I could hear someone playing boules. Clack, then cheering.
Two old men playing chess. Nobody has moved in ten minutes.
I knit on the train, I knit on the bench. Scarf for summer.
I am taking up watercolour. The sea is very patient with me.
Birdsong, cups, a bicycle bell. The afternoon has a band.
The terrier and the cat had a staring contest. A draw.
A gull took a crumb, said thank you, and left. Polite gull.
Is it rude to have a third coffee? Here it seems encouraged.
The light goes gold at five. I plan my walk around it.
A lady just held a door for me and my ice cream. Merci, madame!
The breeze keeps tidying my hair. Very thoughtful of it.
Someone gave me the shady half of the bench. What a kindness.
I'm wandering. Officially. I told the hotel.
Warm stones, cool breeze. Whoever arranged this, thank you.
The waiter remembered my name. I've only said it once!
Left at the fountain, right at the cypress. Or the other cypress.
The afternoon here moves at exactly my speed.
A little boy pointed me to the kiosk. Then he walked me there.
Is this street going somewhere? Wonderful. So am I.
I keep stopping to look at doorways. Each one is a postcard.
Thank you, sun. Thank you, breeze. Thank you, little café.
Lost again. Happily. The map is mostly decoration now.
Late summer has a gold in it. Even at four o'clock.
A lady showed me where the shade starts. Generous of her.
I've walked the promenade twice. It's even nicer the second time.
Everyone says bonjour here. I've said it forty times. Delightful.
The string lights are asleep. I'll come back when they wake.
I thanked the fountain for the cool spray. It splashed back.
My shoes are dusty from the old town. Proper holiday shoes.
The cypresses stand so straight. I'm standing straighter too.
I bought a postcard and then forgot I had. Now I have two.
The air smells of rosemary and sun cream. Heaven, really.
A kind man drew me a map on a napkin. I'm keeping the napkin.
What lovely roofs. Silver on top, white underneath. Like cake.
I meant to buy one peach. The grocer gave me three.
The breeze turned the page of my guidebook. Good suggestion.
Just following the shade from tree to tree. A lovely game.
You have a beautiful town. I hope someone tells you every day.
I've been waved at from a balcony. I waved back with my hat.
The warmth gets right into your shoulders. Like a hug.
The waiter recommended a lemonade. He was entirely correct.
I stopped to let a pigeon cross. We nodded to each other.
Everything is the colour of apricots right now. Marvellous.
A man gave me directions with his whole arm. Very clear.
My plan for today was nothing. It is going beautifully.
A man watering geraniums offered me a spray. I said yes, please!
Strolling, munching a fig, nodding at strangers. A full schedule.
The café saved me the corner seat. They didn't even know me!
A girl on a bike gave me a pastry tip. Taking it immediately.
The wall is warm when you lean on it. I'm leaning on it.
I followed a cat for a while. It knew all the best corners.
The afternoon light makes everyone look like a painting.
My hat and I are going for a walk. My hat is doing great.
A lovely woman lent me her sunglasses for the view. So kind.
I've counted six shades of white so far. All of them nice.
This is the warmest welcome I have ever had from a street.
Just tasting the air. Pine, bread, sea. In that order.
The leaves are making little moving shadows. Very soothing.
Someone told me the fig tree here has a name. I said hello.
I asked a gentleman the time. He said, about lovely o'clock.
The bench was warm from the sun. Like someone kept it for me.
I helped a lady with her shopping bag. She gave me a plum.
I'm walking very slowly so the afternoon lasts longer.
There's a cypress here that looks like it's waving.
Even the shadows are soft here. Lovely, soft shadows.
I picked up a lady's scarf from the breeze. Returned, with a bow.
I complimented a hedge. I believe it grew a little.
Wandering past the café. Breathing in. Not stopping. Yet.
The sea is so blue it looks freshly washed.
A mother offered me a seat at the fountain. Such kindness.
The flowers are all facing the sun. I'm doing the same.
Is it rude to say good afternoon to every single person? No? Good.
I stopped to admire a staircase. Then I climbed it, gently.
Thank you for the shade, palm tree. You're a true gentleman.
A child gave me a seashell. I'll treasure it forever, I said.
The stones of this street are polished by happy feet.
I said I was lost. Three people offered to be lost with me.
The breeze and I have agreed to walk together for a while.
Ambling. I've never ambled before. I'm quite good at it.
There's a lemon on that tree that is simply perfect. Bravo.
A grandmother offered me a cherry from her bag. I took two. Merci!
I am learning to whistle. Two notes so far. Both cheerful.
Today's word is 'flâner'. To stroll with no aim. I'm fluent.
Practising my bonsoir for later. It needs a little more sun.
I'm teaching myself the names of clouds. That one is a lamb.
I learned to tell a fig is ripe. It sort of sighs at you.
My grandfather brought me here when I was six. Same fountain.
I had my first ice cream here, years ago. Pistachio. Still is.
Last summer I danced under those lights. Badly. Gloriously.
I'm practising walking without a map. Going quite well.
I'm learning to sit still. The bench is an excellent teacher.
Lesson one in this town: never rush a lemonade.
I learned the café song. Well, the la-la-la parts.
I'm trying to learn every street name. I'm on number two.
Learning to juggle with three apricots. Eating the evidence.
I practise my French on the pigeons. They never correct me.
My first holiday here, I got lost and found a friend. Odile.
I once watched a whole sunset from that step. Best seat.
Ten summers ago I read my first French book on that step.
I remember the fountain from a photo. It is bigger in person.
My mother bought me a straw hat at that kiosk. I still wear it.
We came every August when I was small. It smells the same.
Practising patience. The figs are not ready. Neither am I.
I've learned the café opens its umbrellas at two. Like flowers.
My Norwegian friend taught me 'koselig'. This street is that.
I'm practising my hello wave. Small, warm, not too eager.
I am trying to walk like the locals. Slower. Slower still.
I've learned which gull is the boss. The one with speckles.
Practising my café order. Un citron pressé, s'il vous plaît.
I learned to skip a stone yesterday. Three hops! A record.
I'm learning the bell rings once for half past. Very tidy.
Yesterday a child taught me hopscotch. I'm on square four.
My first evening here, the string lights came on just for me.
I met my best friend on that very bench. We shared a pear.
Every visit I learn one new shortcut. All of them are longer.
I'm practising saying 'oui' like it's a small song. Oui!
Ten minutes of birdwatching. I know three birds now. Hello.
I'm teaching my feet the hill. They're nearly convinced.
I keep a list of new words. Today: 'parasol'. Very useful.
I learned to fold a napkin into a swan. It looks like a duck.
I'm learning the town's colours. White, blue, and apricot.
My uncle proposed by that fountain. She said oui, of course.
I've learned the trick: order the tarte before you look.
Practising the slow afternoon. It takes all day, happily.
I am learning to tell the cypresses apart. They are all tall.
The first time I came, it rained for a minute. Then gold.
I learned to make a whistle from a grass blade. Pweet!
Practising my balance on the low wall. A little girl clapped.
My grandmother said to bring a good book and no plans. Done.
I'm practising looking up. Balconies, roofs, swallows. Lovely.
I learned the waiter's name is Marcel. Bonjour, Marcel!
I'm working on my sun-squint. It's very French now.
Today's lesson: the shady side of the street is the happy side.
I'm learning to name the herbs by smell. Thyme! Probably.
The first postcard I ever sent was from here. It said wow.
I practise my smile on the shopkeepers. They're all experts.
I learned a card game from two gentlemen. I lost, joyfully.
I'm practising a little rhyme about the fountain. Nearly done.
Learning to eat a peach without a napkin. Not there yet.
I'm practising the art of the long lunch. Hour two going well.
Last year I left my hat on that bench. It was still there!
I'm counting swallows for my nephew. He asked for a report.
A painter taught me to squint to see the colours. It works.
I'm learning the steps to the café dance. Left, left, giggle.
I've learned the sea changes colour every hour. Teal, now.
I'm practising photographs with my eyes. Click. Got it.
Today I'm learning shells. This one is a periwinkle, I think.
I memorised the bakery's opening hours. Proudest thing today.
My first bike ride was on this promenade. Wobbly and happy.
I learned you tap the melon to choose it. I tapped six.
I'm teaching myself to sketch shadows. They keep moving!
I once saw a wedding on these steps. Everyone threw petals.
Learning to say 'encore' properly. For the lemon ice.
Practising my promenade posture. Hands behind back. Like Henri.
My grandmother's café chair is still there. The blue one.
I'm learning the gecko schedule. They come out at three.
Lesson two: say yes when someone offers you a peach.
I remember dancing here with my father, standing on his feet.
I'm practising a new walk. It has a small skip in it.
Learning harmonica. The gulls have been very supportive.
I'm learning to spot the sea between houses. There! And there!
A lady showed me how to tie a scarf the French way. Voilà.
My first word in French was croissant. It got me far.
I'm practising leaving room for dessert. Advanced level.
I learned that the fountain hums if you listen closely.
I'm rehearsing my goodbye. I keep deciding not to use it.
Years ago I wrote my name in the sand here. Still smiling.
Learning to taste olives. This one tastes like sunshine.
My grandson taught me to skip. I'm skipping in secret now.
I'm learning the town by heart. Page one: that blue door.
The day I first came here, I bought two hats. Happy day.
The bougainvillea has gone a deeper pink in this light. Lovely.
I smelled jasmine three streets ago. I am still following it.
Is that a lemon tree? Lit by a lamp? I must sit down.
Pardon, is this the way up? I will take the long way, thank you.
Tomorrow I shall buy a geranium. Today I shall only admire them.
Every doorway here has a pot of something. How do they all agree?
My grandmother grew lemons in tins. She would love this street.
I think I passed this oleander before. It seems pleased to see me.
Plan for tomorrow: croissant, bench, bougainvillea. In that order.
A cat just showed me a shortcut. I did not take it. Too lovely here.
The lemons look like little lamps of their own now.
I have walked in a circle. A very pretty circle.
My mother always said, follow the flowers. I am doing that.
Somebody has watered the planters. The stones still smell of it.
Blue hour, they call it. I would call it blue and lemon hour.
One more street, then up the hill. Possibly two more streets.
The cypresses look like they are standing very politely in line.
I asked a lady about her basil. Now I know her whole family.
I must write to my sister. She will want to come too.
Every corner I turn there is another lemon tree. Generous town.
Tomorrow I will come down earlier. I said that yesterday too.
I have been calling that palm Gérard. I hope it does not mind.
The fountain sounds softer once the lamps are on. Have you noticed?
Little blue door, little blue pot, little white flowers. Perfect.
My father whistles exactly like that man by the café. Uncanny.
Lost again. Happily. The bougainvillea will lead me out.
I counted the window boxes on that street. Eleven. All blooming.
A lemon fell at my feet. I am taking that as a welcome.
Excuse me, which way is the sea? Oh. There. Of course. Thank you.
The rosemary by the steps smells stronger in the evening. Why?
I promised my nephew a postcard of the palms. I will find one.
Even the shadows here are a pleasant colour.
Slowly up, slowly down. I seem to be doing both at once.
There is a fig tree by the church. I am visiting it tomorrow.
When I was small we had a lemon tree. It was a very proud tree.
I keep stopping to smell things. It makes for a slow walk.
What a pretty lamp. And the flowers under it. Oh, and the bench.
My little plan was to walk to the end. I have reached a planter.
Tomorrow: the market, for apricots. My aunt insists on apricots.
Wisteria on a blue shutter. Somebody here has excellent taste.
I think the lavender is getting sleepy. It is leaning a little.
A gentleman tipped his hat at me. I tipped my map back.
The whole town smells of oranges and warm stone. Remarkable.
I have taken a photograph of every geranium. Nearly every one.
My grandfather would have sat on that bench and named the stars.
Pardon, I am just admiring your pots. Carry on. Lovely evening.
In the morning I want to see the lemons wake up. Is that silly?
This street is all bougainvillea. I shall walk it twice.
The sky is the colour of a blue hydrangea. I mean that kindly.
I must remember this. The lamps, the lemons, the little breeze.
I have a small paper map. The town has much better ideas.
Tomorrow I will bring my sketchbook and draw that cypress.
Window box, window box, window box. A lovely rhythm, this lane.
My mother pressed flowers in books. I shall press a petal from here.
The steps here are lined with pots. Like walking up a garden.
Just one more look at the palms, then I am going. Probably.
Plan for tonight: be slow. It is going very well so far.
I said bonsoir to a geranium. Nobody saw. Wonderful.
The olive tree in the square is older than my whole family tree.
Somebody has put a little chair beside their roses. I approve.
The breeze brought me a smell of basil and supper. Merci, breeze.
My brother would climb that fig tree. I will just look at it.
I turned left at the lemons and right at the jasmine. Here I am.
Tomorrow, the walk along the top. Today, the walk along the lamps.
The pots on that balcony are all different blues. How thoughtful.
What do you call the little white flowers? I shall call them nice.
I keep meaning to go home. Then another flower happens.
Every lamp has a moth and every doorstep has a plant. Lovely.
I shall bring my mother here in the spring. For the blossoms.
I found a courtyard full of roses. I did not mean to. Delightful.
Tomorrow morning, I am told, the jasmine is even better.
Back the way I came, but slower. You see more that way.
Is it rude to sniff a stranger's lemon tree? I have done it twice.
A girl gave me a sprig of lavender. It is in my buttonhole now.
The light makes the white walls look like milk with blueberries.
My father planted a palm once. It never got this tall. He laughed.
These cobbles must have walked a thousand visitors home.
I want a balcony like that. Pink flowers, one chair, this view.
Every few steps the smell changes. Lemon, salt, rosemary, bread.
Tonight I shall write in my diary: lemons. Just that word.
Do the palms rustle like that every evening? How very polite.
My little niece would call this a fairy town. She would be right.
I have stopped trying to find my way. It is much nicer like this.
Next visit, a whole summer. I have already told my diary.
The bougainvillea on the post office wall! Somebody loves that wall.
Those flowers close at dusk, I read. Goodnight, little flowers.
Slowly back up the hill. Waving at every lamp on the way.
It is the kind of evening my family would talk about for years.
One last lemon tree. That one. Then the hill. Then supper.
The fountain is still going. It must love an audience.
A cat on the wall just blinked at me. I blinked back. We are friends.
The shutters are closing one by one, like a slow wink.
The clock says twenty to nine. The sky says blue o'clock.
I counted the lamps along the front. I lost count. Lovely.
A gull is standing on one leg. Very elegant of him.
Biscuit just inspected my shoes. I think I passed.
The awnings are rolled up for the night. Tucked in, really.
Is the blue always this blue? I may need a new word.
I took a wrong turn and found a lemon tree. Right turn, then.
The tiles on that roof look like fish scales in this light.
The cat on the wall has not moved in an hour. Admirable.
Every window is a little yellow square. Like a calendar of lamps.
The fountain makes the same sound as a quiet round of applause.
The string lights came on. I said ooh out loud. Twice.
Somebody is watering geraniums by lamplight. How romantic.
The zinc roofs have gone silver. Paris, but with palm trees.
I think the clock tower is smiling. Or that is just the moon.
Wandering is my main activity tonight. I am very good at it.
Biscuit wagged at me. I feel personally welcomed by the town.
The cypresses look like exclamation marks. I agree with them.
Blue hour. Even my linen shirt looks expensive.
One more lap of the fountain. For the fountain's sake.
The palm trees are waving goodnight. I waved back, of course.
Little arrows on the signposts. All of them say this way. Lovely.
The kiosk shutter is half down. Like a sleepy eyelid.
I have walked past the same blue door three times. Still charming.
The fountain lion has a little moss moustache. Very distinguished.
I asked a gull for directions. He pointed with his beak. Sort of.
The sky is doing a gradient. I did not know skies could do that.
A shutter just opened and someone shook out a tablecloth. Charming.
Those striped awnings look like sweets in this light.
The promenade tiles go blue, white, blue. I walk on the white ones.
I tossed a coin in the fountain. I wished for more of this.
The gulls have gone quiet. Even they stop for blue hour.
I found a bench with a view of another bench. Delightful.
The cat on the wall is now a loaf. A very happy loaf.
The bells chimed. I checked my watch. It agreed.
A small plant on every windowsill. Like the houses are wearing hats.
Who paints the shutters this green? I would like to thank them.
I tried to photograph the blue. It came out as merely nice.
Biscuit has found a very interesting leaf. I agree, it is a fine leaf.
The moon is up over the roofs. Right on time.
A gull just landed with great ceremony. Bravo, monsieur gull.
The fountain basin is reflecting the lamps. Two towns for one.
Down the steps, up the steps. The steps seem to enjoy it.
The cat on the wall nodded at me. I am now a local.
There is a tiny lizard on the warm tiles. Bonsoir, little one.
The clock face lights up! The whole town has a night light.
I have decided this lane is my favourite. Also that one.
Someone is playing the accordion somewhere. Very quietly. Perfect.
The awning over the café has one lamp under it. Like a lantern hat.
I said merci to the fountain. It seemed the right thing to do.
Each house has a number in blue tiles. Number nine is very proud.
Biscuit sniffed the fountain, then the lamp, then me. In that order.
Every shutter here has a little heart cut out. I checked four.
Walking along the front. The sea keeps me company on the left.
The fountain splashes in threes. Splash, splash, splash. Like a waltz.
I stopped to tie my shoe and got a view. Excellent trade.
A tiny bell on the bakery door rang hello as I passed.
The bougainvillea looks purple-blue now. Showing off, a little.
I could walk this promenade end to end forever. Perhaps tonight.
The cat on the wall has a friend now. Two loaves.
The lamps are the colour of honey. The sky is the colour of ink.
I got lost and found the fountain. I recommend getting lost.
I just wished on the first star. Then on the second, for luck.
Those little tiles by the door say bienvenue. I feel it.
A cyclist rang her bell at me. I rang back with a hello.
Excuse me, is this the way back? Oh, every way is the way back.
Low wall, warm stone, perfect for sitting. I did not. Next time.
The shutters are lavender here and mint over there. Ice cream town.
Everyone says bonsoir here. I have said it eleven times. Happily.
A gull walked beside me for a bit. A very short tour guide.
The clock just ticked to quarter to. Even the minutes are relaxed.
Little potted rosemary by every step. The whole town smells cooked.
The windows upstairs have lace curtains glowing. Like paper lanterns.
I am wandering with no plan. Best plan I have had all year.
The cat has left the wall. The wall is keeping her spot warm.
The palms are dark against the blue now. Like paper cutouts.
My grandmother had shutters this exact blue. I must tell her.
The fountain is humming to itself. I think it likes the evening.
I leaned on this railing yesterday. I think it remembers me.
The awnings are rolling up one by one. Sleepy eyelids.
Golden hour. Everything here looks freshly polished.
The clock says ten past six. The light says honey.
I counted the zinc roofs from here. Lost count at forty, happily.
My father stood exactly like this. Hands behind, chin up.
Mother always said: find a railing and wait. She was right.
Somebody painted every shutter a different green. Bravo, somebody.
The café floor tiles are little suns. I checked twice.
I came to look at the sea. The sea looked back, very politely.
Pardon, is this golden hour, or is the town just showing off?
I am writing a postcard to my sister. It only says: come.
The cypresses have longer shadows than me. Tall fellows.
My little nephew would love the fountain. He would be in it.
I keep saying merci to people who did nothing. They smile anyway.
The light on the whitewash. I would like it bottled, please.
A railing, a breeze, a view. My entire plan for the evening.
Is there a word for this colour? I shall call it apricot.
The string lights are waiting their turn. Very patient bulbs.
Forty photos of one lemon tree. Each one better than the last.
Grandpa whistled when he was happy. I am whistling, slightly.
The kiosk man waved his newspaper. I waved my map. Friends now.
My map is upside down. The view is the right way up.
The fountain says the same word all evening: splash.
That cat on the warm tiles has the best seat in town.
Every chimney pot is wearing a little gold hat right now.
I lean, therefore I am. On holiday, that counts as philosophy.
The church bell rang six. It took its time about it.
My aunt kept a seashell from a town like this. Now I see why.
Pardon me, I am just admiring your awning. All of them, really.
Half-closed shutters. The houses look like they are napping.
One more minute here. Then one more. That is the routine.
Maman would ask if I brought a jumper. I did. She packed it.
I named the gull on the lamp post Gérard. He has not objected.
The clock tower has a tiny door. Who lives there? I must know.
The railing is warm from the day. Like a teacup you can lean on.
Look at the tiles on that roof. Every one tilted just so.
If I squint, the whole promenade is made of butter.
I sent my brother a photo. He asked which one was me. The happy one.
Golden hour, they call it. I would say golden hours, plural.
The palm tree is waving. At me, I think. I am waving back.
How long is golden hour here? Ah. As long as I like. Merci.
The whitewash goes pink at this hour. Nobody warned me. Wonderful.
My grandfather courted my grandmother at a railing like this.
I took the steps down from the old town. Many steps. Happy ones.
A chair scraped, a cup clinked. The town is tuning up for evening.
Shutters, flowerpots, a bicycle. Every doorway is a still life.
The fountain catches the sun and throws it about. How generous.
I am practising my French on the gulls. They say oui a lot.
There is one tiny lemon on that tree. I am rooting for it.
As a child I thought the sun went to bed in the sea. I still do.
The awning stripes match the sky. Surely that was planned.
The clock is two minutes fast. Everyone is early for the sunset.
Leaning on railings is my best sport. I am a natural.
The light comes in sideways and makes everything look kind.
I promised my daughter a postcard. She gets the whole view.
